17. varaithim paṅtām azôit; literally "leads astray on the road": this refers to the woman and child carried off in raids by enemy hordes, the haênas. varaithim is rendered pun vartakih, whose literal sense is doubtless "in a turning aside," from varet (vertere, p. کرد بدن); the precise sense is given by passages such as gâm varetâm azaiti, "bovem aversum agit, he turns aside and drives off the cattle" (Vd. 14 (44). Que jamais homme ne porte seul un mort²¹ !

Si un homme porte seul un mort, la Nasu²² sort pour le saisir²³ du nez, de l'œil, de la langue, de la mâchoire, de l'organe viril²⁴, de l'anus²⁴ [du mort]. La Druj Nasu se précipite sur lui jusqu'au bout des ongles, et le voici impur pour toujours et à tout jamais²⁵.

Ahura Mazda répondit :

Le lieu de la terre le plus vide d'eau et le plus vide de plantes, dont le sol est le plus net et le plus sec, et par où passent le moins le petit bétail

21. Il s'agit d'un mort dont la Nasu (note suivante) n'a pas été chassée par le Sag-did. L'analyse du Dinkart porte en effet : madam vinâs-î rimanihi min nasâi, ghalic zaki kalbâ lâ khazitûnt, pun tan-âi yadrûnênd : « du péché de souillure contracté en portant seul un cadavre qui n'aurait pas subi le Sag-did ». — Dans toutes les opérations relatives aux funérailles, l'homme ne doit jamais agir isolé : le mort doit être veillé par deux personnes, lavé par deux personnes, porté par deux porteurs ; il faut deux prêtres pour les prières ; les personnes qui suivent la procession vont deux à deux (voir Vd. VIII, Appendice A).

22. Le mot Nasu a deux sens ; il désigne soit le cadavre, le νέκυς, soit le démon, la Druj, qui prend possession du cadavre et dont la présence se marque par la décomposition du corps et l'infection. Au premier sens, nasu est un nom commun, pehlvi nasâi (nésâ) ; au second sens, c'est un nom propre, transcrit en pehlvi nasûsh. — Sur l'expulsion de la Nasu par le Sag-did, voir Vd. VIII, 14-22.

23. upa-raêthwayêiti ; litt. « va se mêler à lui ».

24. fravâkhsha, kir ; le sens primitif est tâk, pallava (Yasna X, 5, 12) : ce sont les deux sens du latin virga. — frashumaka, kûn (frashu- = *frakhshu, *praksu, πρωκτός).

25. Il ne peut se purifier comme le Nasâ-sâlâr ordinaire (Vd. VIII, 13) et il doit vivre pour toujours isolé des fidèles que son contact souillerait. En fait il est « digne de mort » margarzân : « il ressort de l'Avesta, dit le Commentaire, que si, sachant que l'homme est mort et qu'il n'y a pas eu de Sag-did, il le transporte néanmoins, il commet un péché digne de mort » (vinâsi margarzân). La corruption étant plus forte sans Sag-did, il commet le même crime qu'un homme qui introduirait la peste dans le pays.

26. iristô-kasha, litt. « celui qui traîne un mort » : l'expression moderne est nasâ-sâlâr ou plus exactement khandyâ (voir Farg. VIII, Appendice A). Il s'agit ici du Nasâ-sâlâr évak-bar, « qui a porté seul un cadavre ». — Analyse du Dinkart (§ 7) : « sur la nourriture, le vêtement et la place de l'homme qui s'est rendu impur et digne de mort (riman û margarzân) en transportant seul un cadavre (pun nasâi évak-barih râi) ».

38 ANNALS OF THE MUSÉE GUIMET

14 (44). Let no man ever carry a corpse alone²¹!

If a man carries a corpse alone, the Nasu²² rushes out to seize him²³ by the nose, the eye, the tongue, the jaw, the virile organ²⁴, the anus²⁴ [of the dead man]. The Druj Nasu flings herself upon him to the very tips of his nails, and he is henceforth impure forever and for all time²⁵.

15 (49). Creator of the world of bodies, holy!

What is the place where the man who has carried (alone) a corpse²⁶ shall stand?

Ahura Mazda answered:

The place on earth most empty of water and most empty of plants, whose soil is the cleanest and the driest, and where the least small cattle pass

21. This concerns a corpse whose Nasu (see following note) has not been driven out by the Sag-did. The analysis in the Dinkart states: madam vinâs-î rimanihi min nasâi, ghalic zaki kalbâ lâ khazitûnt, pun tan-âi yadrûnênd: "of the sin of defilement contracted by carrying alone a corpse that has not undergone the Sag-did." — In all funeral operations, a man must never act alone: the corpse must be watched by two persons, washed by two persons, carried by two bearers; two priests are required for the prayers; those who follow the procession go two by two (see Vd. VIII, Appendix A).

22. The word Nasu has two meanings; it designates either the corpse, the νέκυς, or the demon, the Druj, who takes possession of the corpse and whose presence is marked by the decomposition of the body and infection. In the first sense, nasu is a common noun, Pahlavi nasâi (nésâ); in the second sense, it is a proper name, transcribed in Pahlavi as nasûsh. — On the expulsion of the Nasu by the Sag-did, see Vd. VIII, 14-22.

23. upa-raêthwayêiti; literally, "goes to mingle with him."

24. fravâkhsha, kir; the primitive meaning is tâk, pallava (Yasna X, 5, 12): these are the two meanings of the Latin virga. — frashumaka, kûn (frashu- = *frakhshu, *praksu, πρωκτός).

25. He cannot purify himself like the ordinary Nasâ-sâlâr (Vd. VIII, 13) and must live forever isolated from the faithful whose contact he would defile. In practice he is "worthy of death" (margarzân): "It follows from the Avesta, says the Commentary, that if, knowing that the man is dead and that no Sag-did has taken place, he transports the body nonetheless, he commits a sin worthy of death" (vinâsi margarzân). The corruption being greater without the Sag-did, he commits the same crime as a man who would introduce the plague into the country.

26. iristô-kasha, literally "one who drags a corpse": the modern expression is nasâ-sâlâr or more exactly khandyâ (see Farg. VIII, Appendix A). This refers to the Nasâ-sâlâr évak-bar, "who has carried a corpse alone." — Analysis from the Dinkart (§ 7): "on the food, clothing, and dwelling of the man who has rendered himself impure and worthy of death (riman û margarzân) by transporting a corpse alone (pun nasâi évak-barih râi)."

34. pāstò-frathaûhem hè kameredhem vināthayen, translated as: pôst pahnâi olâ kamâr anâ (read barâ?) kashind "they will pull the head across the width of the skin" and glossed: aîghash rôishâ barâ paskûnand "that is to say they will sever his head": the "width of the skin" no doubt refers to the neck. Perhaps one should understand: "they will pull his head with the width of the skin," meaning they will flay him alive before beheading him: flaying alive was one of the punishments in fashion in ancient Persia, Achaemenid and Sassanid (cutes vivis hominibus detrahunt, particulatim vel solidas; Ammianus Marcellinus, XXIII; cf. Herodotus, V, 25): Manes was "in the Persian manner" flayed alive, then thrown to the dogs (Theodoret, Contra haeret, I: τὴν Περσικὴν τιμωρίαν). It is in this sense that the Rivâyat of Fraser interprets the parallel passage Farg. IX, 49, note 54. — Cf. Vd. XVIII, 10; Ardâ Virâf, XI, 2; and the Rivâyat cited Farg. VII, 27, note 31 and IX, 50, note 55.

This construction could only be justified if paiti-mithnâiti were neuter or impersonal; but âmithnâiti "he thinks, he says to himself" (mined, ciñtayati, Aog., 53) shows that paiti-mithnâiti has a person as its subject and not a thing: the subject is no doubt avâo "this man," him being the object "this" or perhaps the adverb "here": the Pahlavi renders avâo him as madam danâ damîk "upon this earth"; cf. If a man buries a human corpse or the corpse of a dog, and a full year passes without him disinterring it, what shall be the penalty?

Ahura Mazda answered:

A thousand strokes of the Aspahê-ashtra, a thousand strokes of the Sraoshô-carana.

38 (130). Creator of the corporeal world, holy one!

If a man buries a human corpse or the corpse of a dog, and two years pass without him disinterring it, what shall be the payment, what shall be the expiation, what shall be the purification⁷²?

67. acishtem ahûm, "the worse world," is the opposite of vahishtem ahûm, the excellent world, Paradise. The common name for hell, duzhah, in Pahlavi dûzhakh, literally means "the bad world," duzh-ah(u).

68. Conjectural translation: vispaca avi tighra nimata. The Pahlavi translates: harvisp madam ol tih afgûnâtêt (read afgûninêt), "he causes it to fall upon every tih"; it adds in a gloss: "everywhere it falls, it falls upon tih." What is the meaning of tih? The Munich manuscript translates it as dûzakh, "hell," and tih seems to have this sense in Vd. XIX, 6, 19, apâkhtar tih, translated in the same manuscript اوا خَتَر يَه يعي دوزخ: "âvakhtar is tih, that is to say, hell." tighra literally means "pointed," and تَه "the bottom" may originally have meant "the point." However, the word is also used to refer to a knife (Vd. IX, 10, 21); and one could understand it as meaning "everywhere it falls, it falls upon knives." nimata has the appearance of a noun qualified by tighra, but the Pahlavi reads it as a verb (nam?), and we follow that reading, in the absence of more precise information.

69. Cf. § 8.

70. citha, tójishn; properly applied to monetary expiation; see note 72.

71. See the General Introduction to the Vendidad regarding this formula.

72. These three terms citha, âperetish, yaozhdâthrem are respectively glossed:

Il n'y a pas de payement, pas d'expiation, pas de purification. Son crime est inexpiable pour toujours et à tout jamais 73.

40 (137). Quand en est-il ainsi ?

Quand le coupable appartient à la confession [de Zoroastre] ou qu'il est instruit dans la Religion de Mazda 74.

Si le coupable n'appartient pas à la confession, ou s'il n'est pas instruit dans la Religion de Mazda 75, son crime est emporté 76 s'il fait confession de la Religion de Mazda 77 avec l'intention de ne plus commettre par la suite ces actes de transgression 78.

41 (142) 79. Car la Religion de Mazda, ô Spitama Zarathushtra, emporte 80

tôjishn, pun khvâstak ; pûhr, pun ashtar u srôshôcaranâm ; yôzhdâsrih, pun ravân « payement, en argent ; châtiment, par l'ashtar et le srôshô-carandm ; purification, pour l'âme ».

73. Il sera damné.

74. Il est damné, s'il est soit âstûtô, soit aiwi-sravanô. — 1° âstûtô est le Beh-din, le Zoroastrien qui récite sa profession de foi mazdéenne, l'âstûiti (voir le frastuyê et l'âstuyê ; vol. I, Yasna, XI, 17 ; XII, 8); glose : « s'il est Beh-din et sait que c'est un péché ». — 2° aiwi-sravanô se dit du non-Zoroastrien, de l'Ak-din, qui connait cette prohibition de la Religion, peut-être du catéchiste ; glose : « s'il est Ak-din et commet malicieusement ce crime. » Dans l'un et l'autre cas il y a intention coupable, dans le premier cas par négligence ou impiété, dans l'autre par insulte et défi.

75. S'il est soit anâstûtô, soit anaiwisravanô, c'est-à-dire s'il s'agit, soit d'un non-Zoroastrien bien intentionné (ak-din pun karfak hûskâlt), soit d'un Zoroastrien mal instruit par un impie (la glose signifie littéralement : « un Beh-din qui agit d'après le désir et la demande d'un méchant avec la certitude et l'intention de faire le bien »), et qui par suite se fait des idées fausses sur le bien et le mal : voir les notes 81 et sq.

76. aètacit aèibyô spâoûhaiti : olâshân vinâs min olâshân anshûtâân ramîtûnît, « il rejette ces fautes loin de ces hommes ». — spâoûh, traduit comme spa-y (note 80), dont il est un élargissement.

77. âstavanacîibyô daènâm, âstavânih (construit comme sujet de ramîtûnêt) patitikih : « la confession, c'est-à-dire la récitation de Patet » : le Patet, ou formule de repentir, débute en effet par l'âstuyê (v. infra PATET) : confession de péché et confession de foi sont inséparables, la conscience du péché supposant confession de foi.

78. Glose : « s'il fait Patet en prenant la résolution de ne plus pécher. » Cf. Saddar, XLV : « Il y a pénitence quand on fait pénitence d'un péché commis et qu'on n'en commet pas un nouveau : si on en commet un nouveau, le premier revient. »

79. Dinkart, l. l., § 12 : « De la puissance de la Bonne Religion à enlever le péché de l'homme » (madam zôri shapir Din pun barâ mûshtani vinâs min anshûtâân).

80. spayêiti, litt. ramîtûnêt « jette loin de lui ». Le mot est employé dans la litté-

39 (135). Ahura Mazda replied:

There is no payment, no expiation, no purification. His crime is inexpiable forever and for all time 73.

40 (137). When is this the case?

When the guilty party belongs to the confession [of Zoroaster] or is instructed in the Religion of Mazda 74.

If the guilty party does not belong to the confession, or is not instructed in the Religion of Mazda 75, his crime is carried away 76 if he makes confession of the Religion of Mazda 77 with the intention of no longer committing these acts of transgression in the future 78.

tôjishn, pun khvâstak; pûhr, pun ashtar u srôshôcaranâm; yôzhdâsrih, pun ravân: "payment, in silver; punishment, by the ashtar and the srôshô-carandm; purification, for the soul."

73. He will be damned.

74. He is damned, whether he is âstûtô or aiwi-sravanô. — 1° âstûtô is the Beh-din, the Zoroastrian who recites his Mazdean profession of faith, the âstûiti (see the frastuyê and the âstuyê; vol. I, Yasna, XI, 17; XII, 8); gloss: "if he is Beh-din and knows that it is a sin." — 2° aiwi-sravanô refers to the non-Zoroastrian, the Ak-din, who knows this prohibition of the Religion, perhaps the catechist; gloss: "if he is Ak-din and commits this crime maliciously." In both cases there is culpable intent, in the first case through negligence or impiety, in the other through insult and defiance.

75. If he is anâstûtô or anaiwisravanô, that is to say if it is a matter either of a well-intentioned non-Zoroastrian (ak-din pun karfak hûskâlt), or of a Zoroastrian badly instructed by a wicked person (the gloss signifies literally: "a Beh-din who acts according to the desire and demand of a wicked man with the certainty and intention of doing good"), and who consequently forms false ideas about good and evil: see notes 81 and following.

76. aètacit aèibyô spâoûhaiti: olâshân vinâs min olâshân anshûtâân ramîtûnît, "he throws these faults far from these men." — spâoûh, translated as spa-y (note 80), of which it is an extension.

77. âstavanacîibyô daènâm, âstavânih (construed as subject of ramîtûnêt) patitikih: "the confession, that is to say the recitation of the Patet": the Patet, or formula of repentance, begins indeed with the âstuyê (v. infra PATET): confession of sin and confession of faith are inseparable, consciousness of sin presupposing confession of faith.

78. Gloss: "if he recites the Patet with the resolution to sin no more." Cf. Saddar, XLV: "There is penitence when one does penance for a sin committed and does not commit a new one: if one commits a new one, the first returns."

79. Dinkart, l. l., § 12: "On the power of the Good Religion to remove the sin of man" (madam zôri shapir Din pun barâ mûshtani vinâs min anshûtâân).

80. spayêiti, lit. ramîtûnêt "throws far from him." The word is used in the liter-

rature pehlvie comme terme technique pour désigner le principe de la puissance expiatrice de la religion : cf. vol. I, p. 91, note 57 et Dâdistân, XLI, 9.

83. nasuspaèm, nasûi-nikânîh : « il sait qu'on ne doit pas enterrer des cadavres : mais il s'imagine que si l'on s'arrange de façon à ce que les chiens et les renards ne puissent porter la nasâ dans le feu ou dans l'eau, il fait bonne œuvre » (c'est-dire qu'il s'imagine que la défense d'enterrer n'a pour objet que de protéger l'eau et le feu : il ne sait pas qu'elle vise la terre même).

Glose : « il sait qu'il est permis de prendre de gros intérêts (vakhshi girân), mais il ne sait pas qu'il n'est pas permis de le prendre au-dessus du taux fixé par la religion » (madam min dinik).

of the man who confesses the bond of his sin. It carries away the abuse of trust⁸¹; it carries away the murder of a believer⁸²; it carries away the burial of a corpse⁸³; it carries away an inexpiable crime⁸⁴; it carries away the worst form of usury⁸⁵; it carries away all the sins that one can commit.

If from now on he performs only good deeds⁸⁷, O Spitama Zarathushtra, the good Religion of Mazda brings about perfect expiation.


Pahlavi literature as a technical term for designating the principle of the expiatory power of religion: cf. vol. I, p. 91, note 57 and Dâdistân, XLI, 9.

FARGARD 4

This Fargard is the only one in the Vendidad that belongs to legislation properly so called: it deals with contracts and assaults upon persons.

I a. Classification of contracts according to the value of their object (2); rescission of a contract by payment of the value of the immediately superior contract (3).

I b. Religious responsibility of the family for the violation of a contract by one of its members (4-11).

I c. Punishment of the Mihir-Druj, the one who violates a contract (12-16).

II a. Definition of assaults upon persons called âgerepta (threat), avaoirishta (attack), aredush (blow. — § 17).

II b. Punishment for the threat (18-21), for the attack (22-25), for the blow (26-29); for the blow that wounds (30-33); for the blow that draws blood (34-36); for the blow that breaks a bone (37-39); for the blow that kills (40-43).

III a. The duty of charity toward fellow believers: giving them money, a wife, instruction (44-45).

I d. The gravity of false oath in judicial trial (46).

III b. The dignity of wealth, marriage, and material life (47-49 a).

I d'. The judicial trial: the gravity of false oath (49 b-55).

The numbering of the sections shows the logical arrangement of the fragments. The main difficulty has been caused by a transposition that already exists in the manuscript from which all known manuscripts derive, and which placed § 46 between the section on charity and the corresponding digression on the dignity of material goods. It is this transposition that has made the whole of this part of the Fargard so obscure.

1. He who does not return to the man who claims it the money lent upon his prayer¹ is a thief of the thing lent, is a brigand with regard to the lender²; each day, each night that he keeps within his house, as though it were his own, [the property of another]³.

How many contracts are there before you, Ahura Mazda⁴?

Ahura Mazda replied:
There are six, O holy Zarathusthra.
The first is the contract of word⁴.
The second is the contract of hand⁴.

3. Each day that he keeps it, the crime of theft is renewed. — maêthemnahê, mîhán, defined as darpusht gás, "a stronghold, a place of safety." — The words yaṭ vâ kasvi-kâmcina do not belong to the text; they are a quotation from the Commentary, which assimilates the present case to that of Vd. XVIII, 34.

Le troisième est le contrat pour valeur de mouton⁵.
Le quatrième est le contrat pour valeur de bœuf⁶.
Le cinquième est le contrat pour valeur d'homme⁷.
Le sixième est le contrat pour valeur de terre⁸, d'une bonne terre, fertile et de bon rapport.
3. Le contrat de parole s'exécute par la parole.
Le contrat de main l'efface : l'homme donne en compensation la valeur du contrat de main.
Le contrat de mouton efface [le contrat de main] : il donne en compensation la valeur du contrat de mouton.
Le contrat de bœuf efface [le contrat de mouton] : il donne en compensation la valeur du contrat de bœuf.
Le contrat d'homme efface [le contrat de bœuf] : il donne en compensation la valeur du contrat d'homme.


par simple parole. Ainsi, dans un Rivâyat (Grand Rivâyat, p. 96), Zoroastre demande à Ormazd quel est le plus grand péché et Ormazd répond : « C'est quand deux hommes font un contrat oral, sans témoin entre eux que moi Ormazd ; et l'un des deux manque à sa parole et dit : Je n'en connais rien et l'autre n'a point d'autre témoin que moi. » Le zastâ-marshtô, litt. « fait par frottement de main », serait un contrat formé, soit par simple poignée de main, soit par gestes légaux, comme ceux de la stipulation romaine. Cela expliquerait pourquoi le Commentaire n'évalue pas ces deux contrats en argent, ce qu'il fait pour les quatre suivants. Mais ce n'est là qu'une apparence, car on voit par les sections I b, I c que les six contrats forment une série de valeur ascendante du premier au dernier, ce qui prouve que « parole » et « main » sont l'objet de deux contrats spéciaux, et non la forme possible de tout contrat. On conçoit ce que peut être le contrat de main : c'est le contrat de travail ; on voit moins bien ce que peut être le contrat de parole : serait-ce le contrat du jâdangôi, de l'ukhdhôvacah (Vp. III, note 4), par lequel on s'engage à parler pour autrui.

6. Valeur de 12 stirs (= 48 dirhems) : c'est la valeur minimum d'un bœuf (Farg. VII, note 51), le bœuf de valeur moyenne valant 22 stirs, et le bœuf de qualité supérieure en valant 30 (Farg. VII, notes 51-53).
7. Le Commentaire a « valeur de 500 », sans définir s'il s'agit de stirs ou de dirhems ; l'évaluation suivante prouve qu'il s'agit de dirhems ; par suite, d'une valeur de 125 stirs.
8. « Une valeur au-dessus de 500 zûz » (= 500 dirhems, zûz étant l'araméen pour dirhem : voir note 35).

59                    ANNALS OF THE GUIMET MUSEUM

The third is the contract for the value of a sheep⁵.
The fourth is the contract for the value of an ox⁶.
The fifth is the contract for the value of a man⁷.
The sixth is the contract for the value of land⁸, good land, fertile and productive.
3. The spoken contract is fulfilled by the word.
The hand-contract cancels it: the man gives in compensation the value of the hand-contract.
The sheep-contract cancels [the hand-contract]: he gives in compensation the value of the sheep-contract.
The ox-contract cancels [the sheep-contract]: he gives in compensation the value of the ox-contract.
The man-contract cancels [the ox-contract]: he gives in compensation the value of the man-contract.


by simple word. Thus, in a Rivâyat (Grand Rivâyat, p. 96), Zoroaster asks Ormazd what is the greatest sin and Ormazd answers: "It is when two men make an oral contract, with no witness between them but me, Ormazd; and one of the two breaks his word and says: I know nothing of it, and the other has no witness but me." The zastâ-marshtô, literally "made by rubbing of hands," would be a contract formed either by a simple handshake or by legal gestures, like those of the Roman stipulation. This would explain why the Commentary does not evaluate these two contracts in silver, as it does for the four following ones. But this is only an appearance, for one can see from sections I b, I c that the six contracts form an ascending scale of value from the first to the last, which proves that "word" and "hand" are the subject of two special contracts, and not a possible form of all contracts. One can understand what the hand-contract might be: it is the labor contract; one sees less clearly what the word-contract might be: could it be the jâdangôi, the ukhdhôvacah (Vp. III, note 4), by which one pledges to speak on behalf of another?
5. According to the Commentary, a value of 3 stirs, that is to say 12 dirhems (the stir and the dirhem representing the στατήρ and the δραχμή).
6. Value of 12 stirs (= 48 dirhems): this is the minimum value of an ox (Farg. VII, note 51), an ox of average value being worth 22 stirs, and an ox of superior quality being worth 30 (Farg. VII, notes 51-53).
7. The Commentary gives "value of 500," without specifying whether it refers to stirs or dirhems; the following evaluation proves that it refers to dirhems; consequently, a value of 125 stirs.
8. "A value above 500 zûz" (= 500 dirhems, zûz being the Aramaic word for dirhem: see note 35).

9. La traduction de tout ce paragraphe est conjecturale : la difficulté consiste dans le sens des deux expressions techniques framarezaiti et añtare urvaitya fradathaiti. La première, traduite fráj mâlêt, se dit Farg. III, 42, de l'action du vent qui balaye la paille : elle signifie au propre « enlever en frottant » et au figuré « effacer, annuler » : ainsi il est dit de l'Avesta, vispem tat paiti framerezaiti dushmatemca, « il efface toute les mauvaises pensées » (Vd. pehlvi, ad Westergaard VII, 54). Le Commentaire pehlvi la fait suivre à chacune des cinq formules où elle paraît du nom du contrat immédiatement inférieur, ce qui conduit au sens qu'un contrat est annulé par le contrat immédiatement supérieur, c'est-à-dire que pour se dégager du premier il faut livrer la valeur du second ; c'est ce qu'exprime la seconde expression : « il livre [telle ou telle valeur] selon accord(?) ». Le cas prévu n'est pas celui où l'on viole le contrat, où l'on est mihirdruj, mais celui où l'on veut revenir sur un contrat, le résilier.

10. Littéralement : « combien le contrat violé rend-il coupables » (àstàrayêitê : voir Farg. V, note 7).

11. adha-cithanâm narâm nabànazdish tanâm. Le système de la famille patriarcale, en usage dans la Perse zoroastrienne, entraîne assez naturellement la responsabilité collective de la famille (cf. Dinkart, VIII, 20, 9) : elle s'étendait même au criminel (Ammien Marcellin, XXIII, 6 : Leges apud eos impendio formidatae, et abominatae aliae, per quas ob noxam unius omnis propinquitas perit).

12. satâish : la tradition supplée l'idée d'années : 300 shant bim dârishn « ils ont à craindre durant trois cents ans » ; c'est-à-dire, selon Frâmji, que ses parents devront faire le Patet pour son âme durant trois cents ans. Il s'agirait donc d'une responsabilité religieuse, et non civile — celle-ci d'ailleurs allait de soi et n'avait pas besoin sans doute d'être exprimée. La casuistique semble avoir cherché à réduire le cercle de la responsabilité : « le fils né après le péché a seul à craindre ; les parents vertueux n'ont rien à craindre ; quand le père meurt, le fils vertueux n'a rien à craindre ». Les Rivâyats transférent toute la peine sur le coupable et enseignent qu'il sera dans l'enfer trois cents ans.

1 b.

5 (24). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!

Ahura Mazda replied:

He draws into solidarity with his punishment his nearest relatives¹¹ for three hundred [years]¹².


9. The translation of this entire paragraph is conjectural: the difficulty lies in the meaning of the two technical expressions framarezaiti and añtare urvaitya fradathaiti. The first, translated fráj mâlêt, appears in Farg. III, 42, referring to the action of the wind sweeping away straw: it literally means "to remove by rubbing" and figuratively "to cancel, annul": thus it is said in the Avesta, vispem tat paiti framerezaiti dushmatemca, "it wipes away all evil thoughts" (Vd. Pahlavi, ad Westergaard VII, 54). The Pahlavi Commentary appends it to each of the five formulas where it appears with the name of the immediately lower contract, which leads to the meaning that a contract is canceled by the immediately superior contract, that is to say, in order to free oneself from the first one must deliver the value of the second; this is what the second expression conveys: "he delivers [such and such a value] according to agreement(?)". The case envisaged is not the one where a contract is violated, where one is mihirdruj, but the one where a person wishes to go back on a contract, to rescind it.

10. Literally: "how many does the violated contract render guilty" (àstàrayêitê: see Farg. V, note 7).

11. adha-cithanâm narâm nabànazdish tanâm. The patriarchal family system, in use in Zoroastrian Persia, quite naturally entailed collective family responsibility (cf. Dinkart, VIII, 20, 9): it extended even to criminal matters (Ammianus Marcellinus, XXIII, 6: Leges apud eos impendio formidatae, et abominatae aliae, per quas ob noxam unius omnis propinquitas perit).

12. satâish: tradition supplies the idea of years: 300 shant bim dârishn "they have to fear for three hundred years"; that is to say, according to Frâmji, that his relatives will have to perform the Patet for his soul for three hundred years. This would therefore be a religious responsibility, and not a civil one — the latter went without saying and presumably needed no explicit statement. Legal casuistry seems to have sought to reduce the circle of responsibility: "the son born after the sin alone has cause to fear; virtuous parents have nothing to fear; when the father dies, the virtuous son has nothing to fear." The Rivâyats transfer the entire punishment onto the guilty party and teach that he will be in hell for three hundred years.

Burnouf, 5, p. 154) : âgerepta : grihîtam kila kasya apy upari ghâtamanasâ çastram grihnâti tat pâpam âgraftam : « le saisi: c'est-à-dire saisir une arme avec l'intention de frapper quelqu'un ».
avaoirishta : bhrâmitam, kila kasya apy upari ghâtamanasâ çastram bhrâmayati tat pâpam avâvarastam : « le brandi; c'est-à-dire brandir une arme sur quelqu'un avec l'intention de le frapper ».
aredush : tacca îdricam bhavati, kila çastram yatnatayâ carire evam dadâti yathâ na pîdâm karoti atha ghâtamca îdricam karoti yasya trirâtrâd antare pîdâm upacramati, atha chedamca ânguladvayapramânam bhavati tad api pâpam ardus jneyam : « aredush : asséner l'arme sur le corps sans faire de blessure; ou en faire une qui guérit en trois jours, ou faire une blessure de deux doigts. »
Le Vendidad ne définit que ces trois premiers délits parce que ce sont les seuls qui soient désignés en zend par un nom technique qui ait besoin d'être expliqué : les autres sont désignés par des termes qui se définissent d'eux-mêmes (§§ 30, 34, 37, 40).

Le mot tanâfûhr vient du zend tanu-peretha, plus souvent employé sous la forme peshô-tanu (= peretô-tanu) : le peshôtanu ou tanâfûhr est le criminel puni de deux cents coups d'Aspahê-ashtra ; voir l'Introduction générale du Vendidad.

Burnouf, 5, p. 154): âgerepta: grihîtam kila kasya apy upari ghâtamanasâ çastram grihnâti tat pâpam âgraftam: "the seized: that is to say, seizing a weapon with the intention of striking someone."
avaoirishta: bhrâmitam, kila kasya apy upari ghâtamanasâ çastram bhrâmayati tat pâpam avâvarastam: "the brandished; that is to say, brandishing a weapon over someone with the intention of striking them."
aredush: tacca îdricam bhavati, kila çastram yatnatayâ carire evam dadâti yathâ na pîdâm karoti atha ghâtamca îdricam karoti yasya trirâtrâd antare pîdâm upacramati, atha chedamca ânguladvayapramânam bhavati tad api pâpam ardus jneyam: "aredush: to strike the weapon against the body without causing a wound; or to cause one that heals within three days, or to cause a wound of two fingers' breadth."

Il s'agit du fameux hérésiarque communiste qui fut un instant au pouvoir sous le règne de Kôbâd (488-531) et qui fut mis à mort sous Noshirvan. On ne voit pas ailleurs qu'il ait prêché l'abstinence et le jeûne : selon Albîrûni (Chronology, 192), il défendait d'égorger le bétail avant qu'il fût arrivé au terme naturel de la vie. D'après Firdausi et Shahristâni, Mazdak partait de ce principe que le besoin, niyâz, et la convoitise, âz, sont le principe de tous les maux sociaux : il y remédiait en supprimant la propriété individuelle : il n'est pas étonnant qu'il ait aussi essayé de réfréner l'appétit.

I d'.

49 b (142). The first time he commits this crime without waiting for a second offense 40,

36. Astô-vidhôtu, the Demon of death; see Farg. V, 8, note 13. The man who eats has more vital force.

37. ishush hvâthakhtô, tir hûsakht, literally "well arranged": cf. Farg. IX, 43.

38. The Commentary gives as an example Zarhûn-dât: the name is unfortunately too corrupted to allow a historical identification.

39. The heretic who advocates fasting (cf. n. 34), "like Mazdak, son of Bàmdàd," says the Commentary. This refers to the famous communist heresiarch who was briefly in power during the reign of Kôbâd (488–531) and was put to death under Noshirvan. It is not attested elsewhere that he preached abstinence and fasting: according to Albîrûni (Chronology, 192), he forbade the slaughter of livestock before it had reached the natural end of its life. According to Firdausi and Shahristâni, Mazdak held the principle that need, niyâz, and greed, âz, are the source of all social evils: he remedied this by abolishing private property, so it is not surprising that he also attempted to curb appetite.

The Commentary places the four clauses beginning with yasca in symmetry with aêshô zi narô: "For this man fights against the attacks of Astô-vidhôtu, and so too does the one who fights against the well-aimed arrow; and the one who fights against winter...; and the one who fights against the tyrant...; and the one who fights against the Ashemaogha, the impious one of the just." The obscure gloss that follows does not refer to Mazdak, but to the faithful man whom one has in mind, "who has satisfied himself (manash nafshâ sir vashtamûnt; ms. Paris, no. 26), while the other has given himself over to hunger and death."

40. The false oath (v. § 54): while other crimes are only punished with the extreme penalty after a repeat offense (v. §§ 20, 24, 28, etc.), this one is punished with the maximum from the very first offense. This concerns the false oath taken in a judicial ordeal, the Var. These ordeals were numerous, thirty-three in number, it is said (Ardâ Virâf, ed. Haug, p. 145; cf. Dinkart in the Pahlavi Texts, IV, the passages indexed under the word Ordeal). 50 (143). His crime shall be treated there below⁴¹ with the worst punishments known here below: as if with bronze knives one were to cut his perishable body limb from limb⁴², or worse still.

51 (146). His crime there below shall be treated with the worst punishments known here below: as if the limbs of his perishable body were to be bound with bronze chains⁴³, or worse still.

52 (149). His crime there below shall be treated with the worst punishments known here below: as if he were forced to throw himself from a height of a hundred men⁴⁴, or worse still.

54 (154). His crime there below shall be treated with the worst punishments known here below, the man who, before the water of sulfur and gold, before the water that knows⁴⁶,

conde, the ordeal to which Adarbâd Mahraspand submitted himself, in order to establish orthodoxy by a clear sign — molten bronze was poured upon the chest. The Sôgand Nâma, or Book of the Oath (Grand Rivâyat), adapting the practice to modern weakness, substitutes boiling milk for molten bronze.
According to the Sôgand Nâma, the ordeal only takes place as a last resort and when both parties demand it: each commits in writing, before proceeding, to pay the other, should they fail, four times the value in dispute. — Beyond the passages cited in the first volume (p. 227, note 15), the Avesta again alludes to the Var in the Yasht of Rashn, § 3, and Afrin Gâhânbâr, § 9.
41. avatha, tamman "there below," in the other world. Literally: "There below this crime is dealt with in the manner one knows in this corporeal world": the sequel proves that it concerns punishments.
42. The punishment inflicted by Parysatis on Roxane: τὴν Ρωξάνην ζῶσαν κατατεμεῖν (PLUTARCH, Artaxerxes).
43. Perhaps better: "if one nailed his body... with bronze nails" (fshé-bish ...ava-pasât).
44. vaèmem, vim; cf. Farg. VII, note 8.
45. pârem marezem, parantûm marz. I cannot extract anything from the gloss. Frâmji seems to understand that it concerns blows with a stick.
46. Before undergoing the ordeal of the Var and taking the oath, the litigant who takes it must drink a cup containing, says the Sôgand Nâma, water, narmîna (? زمینه), incense, sulfur (اندکی مایه گوگود), jujube (سجب), and a dânak of gold in solution (دانك مایه زر آب).

Si un homme devant l'eau de soufre et d'or, devant l'eau qui sait, vient, sachant son mensonge, se réclamer de Rashnu et mentir à Mithra, quelle sera la peine ?

سوکند خوردن ayant signifié d'abord « boire du soufre »). — zaranyàvaitim répond au زرآب. — vithushavaitim, cihrân-ômand, est moins clair ; on ne voit pas si vithusha désigne un des éléments de ces ὕδατα ὄρχια ou si l'épithète est d'ordre moral : c'est dans ce dernier sens que je la prends à cause de la symétrie du mot avec draoghem-vithush : elle sait qu'il ment comme il le sait lui-même : le pehlvi semble signifier « qui a manifestation ».

47. paitisanhem Rashnaosca : il se réclame de Rashnu, le Génie de la véracité (Yasht XII), littéralement : il va « en protestation de véridique » ou « en protestation de Rashnu ». 55 (156). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!

If a man comes before the water of sulfur and gold, before the water that knows, knowing his lie, to invoke Rashnu and lie to Mithra, what shall be the punishment?

Ahura Mazda answered:

Seven hundred strokes of the Aspahê-ashtra, seven hundred strokes of the Sraoshô-carana.

سوکند خوردن having first meant "to drink sulfur"). — zaranyàvaitim corresponds to زرآب. — vithushavaitim, cihrân-ômand, is less clear; one cannot tell whether vithusha designates one of these ὕδατα ὄρχια or whether the epithet is of moral order: it is in this latter sense that I take it, on account of the symmetry of the word with draoghem-vithush: it knows that he lies just as he knows it himself: the Pahlavi seems to mean "one who has manifestation."

47. paitisanhem Rashnaosca: he invokes Rashnu, the Genius of truthfulness (Yasht XII), literally: he goes "in protestation of the truthful one" or "in protestation of Rashnu." Pahlavi: "he says: I speak the truth." — Here is the oath formula, according to the Sógand Nâma: "Before Bahman, the Amshaspand; before Ardibahisht the Amshaspand, here lit before me; before Shahrivar the Amshaspand, placed before me; before Isfandârmat the Amshaspand, who is beneath my feet; before Khordad the Amshaspand, placed before me; before Amardâd, the Amshaspand, who is before me and whom I am about to drink: I swear, by the soul and the Fravashi of Zardusht Isfintamàn, by the soul of Adarbâd Mahraspandàn, by the soul and the Fravashis of all the righteous who are and who have been, that I have nothing of yours, such son of such a one; and have no knowledge of having received anything in the way of gold, silver, metal, bodily garment, nor any of the objects created by the creator Ormazd": cf. the Avestan formula, note 28.

48. Mithra is the god of the contract (see Mihir Yasht): his very name, as a common noun, means "contract": one who violates a contract is called Mithrô-druj, Mihir-druj, "liar to Mithra." On his role as judge in the underworld, in company with Rashnu, see Mihir Yasht and Rashn Yasht.

FARGARD 5

Ce Fargard et les suivants, jusqu'au douzième inclusivement, traitent en particulier de l'impureté contractée par le contact d'un mort et des moyens de ramener la personne ou l'objet souillé à l'état de pureté.

I (1-7). Si un homme involontairement souille le feu (I a, 1-4) ou l'eau (I b, 5-7) en y portant inconsciemment de la matière morte (nasu), il n'entre pas en état de péché.

II (8-9). Innocence du feu (II a, 8) et de l'eau (II b, 9), qui semblent quelquefois tuer, mais ne tuent pas.

III a (10-14). Comment disposer du corps des morts en hiver, quand il est impossible de les porter au Dakhma.
III b (15-20). Pourquoi Ahura, qui défend à l'homme de souiller l'eau, fait tomber l'eau du ciel sur les Dakhmas chargés de cadavres, pour les purifier.
III c (21-26). Excellence de la pureté et valeur suprème de la partie de la Loi zoroastrienne qui enseigne les moyens de purification.

IV (27-38 = Farg. VI, 6-9). L'aire de contagion de la Druj Nasu (le démon de corruption caché dans les cadavres) est plus ou moins large selon que la vertu du mort le met plus ou moins haut dans l'échelle des êtres.

V (39-44). Purification des instruments du sacrifice souillés par contact avec la nasu.

translation:
FARGARD 5

This Fargard and the following ones, up to and including the twelfth, deal in particular with the impurity contracted through contact with a dead person, and with the means of restoring a person or object that has been defiled to a state of purity.

I (1-7). If a man involuntarily defiles fire (I a, 1-4) or water (I b, 5-7) by unknowingly bringing dead matter (nasu) into contact with them, he does not enter into a state of sin.

II (8-9). The innocence of fire (II a, 8) and water (II b, 9), which sometimes seem to kill, but do not actually kill.

III a (10-14). How to dispose of the bodies of the dead in winter, when it is impossible to carry them to the Dakhma.
III b (15-20). Why Ahura, who forbids man to defile water, causes rain to fall from the sky upon the Dakhmas laden with corpses, in order to purify them.
III c (21-26). The excellence of purity and the supreme value of that part of the Zoroastrian Law which teaches the means of purification.

IV (27-38 = Farg. VI, 6-9). The area of contagion of the Druj Nasu (the demon of corruption hidden within corpses) is greater or lesser depending on how high the virtue of the deceased places him in the scale of beings.

V (39-44). Purification of sacrificial instruments defiled by contact with the nasu.

VI (45-62 = VII, 60-72). Traitement de la femme qui accouche d'un en-
fant mort-né ; ce que l'on doit faire de ses vêtements.

I a.

1. Un homme meurt dans les profondeurs de la vallée¹ : un oiseau prend
son vol des hauteurs de la montagne vers les profondeurs de la vallée ; il
se repaît du corps de l'homme qui vient de mourir : puis l'oiseau reprend
son vol des profondeurs de la vallée vers les hauteurs de la montagne. Il
va sur un arbre, un des arbres à bois dur ou des arbres à bois tendre² et
sur cet arbre il vomit et fait des ordures³.

2 (7). Or voici qu'un homme monte des profondeurs de la vallée vers les
hauteurs de la montagne. Il arrive à l'arbre où [est allé] l'oiseau⁴ : il veut
prendre du bois pour le feu. Il abat l'arbre, il le découpe, il le taille⁵ ; il
l'allume dans le feu, fils d'Ahura Mazda. Quelle sera sa peine⁶ ?

3 (11). Ahura Mazda répondit :

Jamais Nasu apportée par le chien, apportée par les oiseaux, apportée
par le loup, apportée par le vent ne met l'homme en état de péché⁷.

4 (12). Si la Nasu apportée par le chien, apportée par les oiseaux, appor-
tée par le loup, apportée par le vent, pouvait mettre l'homme en état de

1. jãfnavò raonam, littér. « les profondeurs des plaines »; glose « c'est-à-dire les
profondeurs [d'en bas] de la montagne » (zafrih min kóf).

2. khraozhdvanãm, sakht : « par exemple l'amandier » (vani vâtâm); varedvanãm,
narm (cf. sscr. vrand-in) : « par exemple le saule » (vit).

3. irita, rit (M. می کند شاشد), ordures liquides; paitita, ordures solides.

4. upa tãm vanãm aèiti yãm hô mereghô, litt. « arborem accedit quam illa avis ».

5. janaiti, makhitûnêt (pun bun), « il l'abat (par la racine) »; thweresaiti, paskûnêt
tâk tâk, « il le coupe, pièce à pièce »; tashti, tâshêt « il le taille » (en bûches).

6. Pour avoir apporté au feu du bois souillé de Nasâ, contrairement à la règle :
« dâyata dâitya pairishta, donnez du bois normal et bien examiné » (cf. vol. I, 390,
n. 29). Pour la purification du bois, voir Vd. VII, 28 sq.

translation:
66 ANNALS OF THE MUSÉE GUIMET

VI (45-62 = VII, 60-72). Treatment of the woman who gives birth to a stillborn child; what must be done with her clothing.

I a.

1. A man dies in the depths of the valley¹: a bird takes flight from the heights of the mountain toward the depths of the valley; it feeds on the body of the man who has just died; then the bird takes flight again from the depths of the valley toward the heights of the mountain. It alights on a tree, one of the hardwood trees or the softwood trees,² and on that tree it vomits and leaves its droppings.³

2 (7). Now it happens that a man climbs from the depths of the valley toward the heights of the mountain. He arrives at the tree where the bird has been⁴: he wants to take wood for the fire. He fells the tree, cuts it up, and splits it⁵; he lights it in the fire, O son of Ahura Mazda. What will his penalty be?⁶

3 (11). Ahura Mazda answered:

Never does the Nasu brought by the dog, brought by the birds, brought by the wolf, brought by the wind place a man in a state of sin.⁷

4 (12). If the Nasu brought by the dog, brought by the birds, brought by the wolf, brought by the wind, could place a man in a state of

1. jãfnavò raonam, literally "the depths of the plains"; gloss: "that is to say the depths [from below] of the mountain" (zafrih min kóf).

2. khraozhdvanãm, sakht: "for example the almond tree" (vani vâtâm); varedvanãm, narm (cf. Sanskrit vrand-in): "for example the willow" (vit).

3. irita, rit (M. می کند شاشد), liquid waste; paitita, solid waste.

4. upa tãm vanãm aèiti yãm hô mereghô, literally "he approaches the tree which that bird visited."

5. janaiti, makhitûnêt (pun bun), "he fells it (by the root)"; thweresaiti, paskûnêt tâk tâk, "he cuts it, piece by piece"; tashti, tâshêt "he splits it" (into logs).

6. For having brought to the fire wood defiled by Nasâ, contrary to the rule: "dâyata dâitya pairishta, bring wood that is normal and well examined" (cf. vol. I, 390, n. 29). For the purification of wood, see Vd. VII, 28 ff.

7. âstârayèiti, âstârînêt, that is to say "does not make guilty" (vinâskâr lâ obdûnênd): cf. anâstaretò, translated in the Farhang zend-pehlvi as a-vinâs, "without fault, innocent"; âstâr is translated in the Minôkhard (II, 33) as dosha "fault," and corresponds in Judeo-Persian translations to the Hebrew פשע, sin, crime (cf. Études iraniennes, II, 135). — Cf. Derenbourg, Essai sur l'histoire de la Palestine, 196, note 1.

péché, bien vite, tout ce monde des corps que j'ai créé ne serait plus qu'un seul criminel, désireux de détruire le bien⁸ et dont l'âme gémira un jour⁹, à cause du nombre infini d'êtres qui meurent sur la face de cette terre.


I b.

5 (15). Créateur du monde des corps, saint !
Un homme irrigue un champ de blé. Le courant¹⁰ vient une fois, il vient deux fois, il vient trois fois : à la quatrième fois, un chien, un renard ou un loup y traînent de la Nasu. Quelle sera la peine de l'homme ?
6 (19) Ahura Mazda répondit :
Jamais Nasu apportée par le chien, apportée par les oiseaux, apportée par le loup, apportée par le vent ne met l'homme en état de péché¹¹.
7 (20). Car si la Nasu apportée par le chien, apportée par les oiseaux, apportée par le loup, apportée par le vent, mettait l'homme en état de pé-ché, bien vite tout ce monde des corps que j'ai créé ne serait plus qu'un seul criminel, désireux de détruire le bien et dont l'âme gémira un jour, à cause du nombre infini d'êtres qui meurent sur la face de cette terre.


II a.

8 (23). Créateur du monde des corps, saint !


8. ishasemjit-ashem... peshôtanush : imité et rajeuni, quant à la forme, d'un vers des Gâthas (LIII, 9 b) : aêshascâ déjit-aretâ peshôtanvô, « criminels désireux de détruire le bien » (l'Asha). — peshôtanu est généralement employé dans le Vendidad dans le sens technique : ici il a encore son sens primitif, margarzân « criminel digne de mort ». — ishasemjit-ashem est une construction absolue, « en désir de détruire l'asha » : remarquer areta = asha.
9. khraozhdat-urva ; son âme gémira quand elle sera repoussée du Paradis : imité des Gâthas (Yasna XLVI, 11 c ; Ll, 13 b; cf. Vd. XIII, 8-9).
10. ana tâ vaidhim ayâo, zaki pun olâshân jûi rapad ; d'après le pehlvi, ana se rapporte à l'eau, tâ au champ : vaidhim = jûi ; ayâo semble être un nominatif de participe présent. Il s'agit sans doute de l'eau d'un canal qui s'ouvre et se ferme.
11. Supposant qu'il a pris au préalable les précautions ordinaires et qu'avant de lancer l'eau dans les canaux il les a soigneusement examinés pour voir s'il y a de la Nasu (Saddar, LXXV).
translation:
ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — FARGARD 5          67

sin, very quickly all this world of bodies that I have created would be nothing more than a single criminal, desirous of destroying the good⁸ and whose soul will groan one day⁹, because of the infinite number of beings who die on the face of this earth.


I b.

5 (15). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!
A man irrigates a wheat field. The current¹⁰ comes once, it comes twice, it comes three times: at the fourth time, a dog, a fox, or a wolf drags Nasu there. What shall be the man's punishment?
6 (19) Ahura Mazda replied:
Never does Nasu brought by the dog, brought by the birds, brought by the wolf, brought by the wind put a man in a state of sin¹¹.
7 (20). For if the Nasu brought by the dog, brought by the birds, brought by the wolf, brought by the wind, were to put a man in a state of sin, very quickly all this world of bodies that I have created would be nothing more than a single criminal, desirous of destroying the good and whose soul will groan one day, because of the infinite number of beings who die on the face of this earth.


II a.

8 (23). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!


8. ishasemjit-ashem... peshôtanush: imitated and renewed, in terms of form, from a verse of the Gathas (LIII, 9 b): aêshascâ déjit-aretâ peshôtanvô, "criminals desirous of destroying the good" (the Asha). — peshôtanu is generally used in the Vendidad in its technical sense: here it still retains its primitive meaning, margarzân, "criminal worthy of death." — ishasemjit-ashem is an absolute construction, "in desire of destroying the asha": note areta = asha.
9. khraozhdat-urva; his soul will groan when it is turned away from Paradise: imitated from the Gathas (Yasna XLVI, 11 c; Ll, 13 b; cf. Vd. XIII, 8-9).
10. ana tâ vaidhim ayâo, zaki pun olâshân jûi rapad; according to the Pahlavi, ana refers to the water, tâ to the field: vaidhim = jûi; ayâo appears to be a nominative participle. It is no doubt referring to the water of a canal that opens and closes.
11. Assuming that he has taken the ordinary precautions beforehand and that before letting the water into the canals he has carefully examined them to see whether there is any Nasu (Saddar, LXXV).

12. Question qui inquiétait les théologiens et alimentait souvent les controverses. L'eau et le feu sont sacrés, ils sont l'œuvre d'Ahura, de qui ne vient que la vie, et pourtant ils font périr, comme s'ils venaient d'Ahriman. « Qu'un Guèbre allume le feu pendant cent ans, disait Saadi; s'il y tombe à la fin, il y brûlera » :

Les chrétiens, dans leurs polémiques avec les prêtres zoroastriens, se moquaient fort de l'ingratitude du feu : « Nos mains, fait dire Élisée un mage, sont devenues dures et calleuses à force de manier la hache, notre dos est courbé sous le faix du bois, nos yeux sont rouges et toujours mouillés par l'âcreté de la fumée qui s'en échappe. Si nous lui jetons beaucoup d'aliments, il s'en affame de plus en plus; si nous ne lui en donnons point du tout, il s'éteint. Si nous nous approchons de lui pour l'adorer, il nous brûle sans le moindre égard; si nous ne nous approchons pas, il se réduit en cendre » (trad. Garabed, p. 211).
— vâ, dans l'interrogation âfsh narem jainti vâ, signifie littéralement « ou bien » et oppose l'idée exprimée à une idée sous-entendue et qui est l'idée positive de celui qui parle : « N'est-ce pas, l'eau ne tue pas ? Ou bien serait-ce par hasard qu'elle tue ? ». Réponse attendue : « Non, certes ». — Ceci donne le sens primitif de l'interrogatif persan âyâ آیا, num, qui n'est que la forme pleine de yâ (parsi ayâo): cf. Journal asiatique, 1883, I, 110.
13. Astô-vidhôtu, Ast-vahât, le Démon de la mort. Le Grand Bundahish l'identifie au Mauvais Vâi dont la mention suit : « Asti-vahât est le mauvais Vâi qui prend la vie [de l'homme]: quand il passe sa main sur l'homme, c'est la Léthargie (Bûshasp: cf. Vd. XI, 9); quand il jette sur lui son ombre (sâyak?), c'est la Fièvre; quand il le regarde dans l'œil, il détruit la vie et on l'appelle Mort » (XXVIII, 35). — Cf. Vd. IV, 49. Son nom semble signifier littéralement « qui défait le corps ».
14. baṅdayêiti, le lie, c'est-à-dire le paralyse: peut-être y a t-il transport sur Astô-vidhôtu des attributs de Vizaresha et s'agit-il du lacet que Vizaresha lance autour du cou de l'homme (voir Vd. XIX, 29 note).
15. Vaya, ou plus correctement Vayu, est, malgré l'assimilation du Grand Bundahish (note précédente), distinct d'Astô-vidhôtu. Il y a deux Vayu, un bon et un mauvais, l'un qui porte au Paradis, l'autre à l'Enfer. Sur Vayu, voir Yasht XV, Introduction.
16. L'eau n'a donc rien à faire avec le meurtre de l'homme : c'est Astô-vidhôtu le coupable. « Rien de ce que j'ai créé dans le monde, dit Ormazd, ne fait de mal aux hommes. C'est le mauvais Nâi [fausse lecture du pehlvi Vâi] qui tue les mortels, qui retire de leur corps sang et âme » (Grand Rivâyat, 124).

68 ANNALS OF THE GUIMET MUSEUM

Does water kill?
Ahura Mazda replied:
It is not water that kills. Asto-vidhotu binds man; once bound, Vayu carries him off. Water pushes him to the surface, water pushes him to the depths, water

12. A question that troubled theologians and frequently fed controversy. Water and fire are sacred; they are the work of Ahura, from whom only life comes, and yet they cause death, as if they came from Ahriman. "If a Zoroastrian lights a fire for a hundred years," said Saadi, "should he fall into it at the end, it will burn him":

If one lights fire for a hundred years, should he fall into it even for a moment, it will burn him.

Christians, in their polemics with Zoroastrian priests, mocked the ingratitude of fire: "Our hands," as Elisée has a mage say, "have grown hard and calloused from wielding the axe, our backs are bent under the weight of the wood, our eyes are red and constantly watering from the sharpness of the smoke that pours out. If we feed it abundantly, it only grows hungrier; if we give it nothing at all, it goes out. If we draw near to worship it, it burns us without the slightest regard; if we do not draw near, it reduces itself to ash" (trans. Garabed, p. 211).
— vâ, in the interrogative phrase âfsh narem jainti vâ, literally means "or else" and sets the expressed idea against an implied one, which is the positive idea of the speaker: "Is it not the case that water does not kill? Or else could it be by chance that it does?" The expected answer is: "No, certainly not." — This gives the primitive sense of the Persian interrogative âyâ آیا, num, which is nothing but the full form of yâ (Parsi ayâo): cf. Journal asiatique, 1883, I, 110.
13. Astô-vidhôtu, Ast-vahât, the Demon of death. The Grand Bundahish identifies him with the Evil Vâi, whose mention follows: "Asti-vahât is the evil Vâi who takes the life [of man]: when he passes his hand over a man, it is Lethargy (Bûshasp: cf. Vd. XI, 9); when he casts his shadow (sâyak?) upon him, it is Fever; when he looks him in the eye, he destroys life and is called Death" (XXVIII, 35). — Cf. Vd. IV, 49. His name seems to mean literally "he who undoes the body."
14. baṅdayêiti, "he binds," that is, he paralyzes: perhaps some of Vizaresha's attributes have been transferred to Astô-vidhôtu, and this refers to the noose that Vizaresha throws around the neck of man (see Vd. XIX, 29, note).
15. Vaya, or more correctly Vayu, is, despite the identification made in the Grand Bundahish (preceding note), distinct from Astô-vidhôtu. There are two Vayu, one good and one evil, one who carries men to Paradise and the other to Hell. On Vayu, see Yasht XV, Introduction.
16. Water therefore has nothing to do with the killing of man: it is Astô-vidhôtu who is guilty. "Nothing that I have created in the world," says Ormazd, "does harm to men. It is the evil Nâi [a misreading of the Pahlavi Vâi] who kills mortals and draws blood and soul from their bodies" (Grand Rivâyat, 124).

Now, nothing I have given to the world shall bring harm to mankind,
But the Nay kills men worse, drawing their veins and souls from their bodies.

17. paiti-raècayèiti. Traduction conjecturale. Le pehlvi semble avoir lu paiti-raè-thwayèiti, car il traduit patirag gûmikhtêt « va se méler à lui » avec la glose : aigh pun sûrák lakhvâr ozalûnêt, laquelle semble signifier « il passe par les ouvertures [du corps] ». II b.

9 (29). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!
Does fire kill?
Ahura Mazda replied:
Fire does not kill. Astô-vîdhôtu binds the man; and thus bound, Vayu carries him off, and fire consumes the mixture of bone and life¹⁹. When he departs from here, it is by Destiny that the thing comes to pass.


III a.

10 (34). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!
If summer has passed and winter is here, what shall the worshippers of Mazda do²⁰?
Ahura Mazda replied:
In each house, in each village, they shall raise three chambers for the dead²¹.


17. paiti-raècayèiti. Conjectural translation. The Pahlavi appears to have read paiti-raè-thwayèiti, for it translates patirag gûmikhtêt "to mingle with him" with the gloss: aigh pun sûrák lakhvâr ozalûnêt, which seems to mean "he passes through the openings [of the body]." The reading paiti-raècayèiti can also lead to this meaning.
18. Or perhaps, "that he departs," meaning he dies. — athra adhât frajasaiti bakhta adhât nijasaiti: frajas and nijas are synonyms, both glossed bará yâtûnêt, that is اىl "he goes away." Gloss: "it is by the path of Destiny that he goes away." — Analysis from the Dinkart, l. l., § 19: madam margîh-î pun vahán-î mayá uá-tâsh, lâ mayá u-âtásh, bará min shédán pun barin yahvûnêt "of the death produced by water and fire: it is not the water and the fire [that produce it]; it comes from demons through Destiny" (barîn is not the Persian جرى sublime; for جرى comes from the preposition bar, which in Pahlavi is apar; it comes from barh "destiny").
19. asta ushtânemca, tan ján; that is, the human form, the body (kâlpût).
20. If a man dies during a season when conditions prevent transporting the body to the Dakhma. Farg. VIII, 4 sq. treats the same subject, but differently.
21. kata, katak, properly "house": there are three of them, one for men, one for women, one for children (cf. Farg. VIII, Appendix A). Like all the hou-

11 (37). Créateur du monde des corps, saint !
De quelles dimensions seront ces chambres pour les morts ?
Ahura Mazda répondit :
Assez grandes pour ne pas heurter la tête de l'homme s'il était debout, ni les pieds étendus ni les bras tendus 22 : telle est régulièrement la chambre des morts 23.

12 (41). Et là ils déposeront le corps inanimé, deux nuits durant, trois nuits durant, ou un mois durant 24, jusqu'à ce que les oiseaux reprennent leur vol 25, les plantes leur poussée, les eaux cachées leur course 26, et que le vent dessèche la terre 27.

13 (44). Et quand les oiseaux reprendront leur vol, les plantes leur poussée, les eaux cachées leur course et que le vent desséchera la terre, alors les adorateurs de Mazda exposeront le corps, le regard au soleil 28.

sons ne sont pas assez considérables ou assez riches pour avoir ces trois constructions, le village aura trois chambres communes pour les morts. Ce sont ces chambres isolées que l'on appelait Zád-marg (Anquetil, Zend Avesta, II, 583). Les quartiers parsis en Perse ont encore de ces maisons communes où chaque famille porte ses morts avant de les transporter au Dakhma, et dans l'Inde même l'usage subsiste encore dans les Mofussil du Gujrate, où on les appelle Nasá-khâna نساخانه « maison de cadavres ». A Bombay et dans les grandes villes il n'y a plus de Zád-marg et le nom de Nasá-khâna est donné au dépôt des pompes funèbres : on dispose du corps suivant les méthodes plus économiques du Farg. VIII, 8.

11 (37). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!
What dimensions shall these chambers for the dead have?
Ahura Mazda replied:
Large enough that a man standing upright would not hit his head, nor stretch out his feet, nor extend his arms 22: such is the standard size of a chamber for the dead 23.

12 (41). And there they shall lay the lifeless body, for two nights, for three nights, or for a month 24, until the birds resume their flight 25, the plants their growth, the hidden waters their course 26, and the wind dries the earth 27.

13 (44). And when the birds resume their flight, the plants their growth, the hidden waters their course, and the wind dries the earth, then the worshippers of Mazda shall expose the body, face turned toward the sun 28.

are not wealthy enough to have these three structures, the village will have three communal chambers for the dead. These are the isolated chambers that were called Zád-marg (Anquetil, Zend Avesta, II, 583). Parsi quarters in Persia still have these communal houses where each family brings its dead before transporting them to the Dakhma, and in India the practice still survives in the Mofussil areas of Gujarat, where they are called Nasá-khâna نساخانه, "house of corpses." In Bombay and in large cities there are no longer any Zád-marg, and the name Nasá-khâna is given to the funeral home: the body is handled according to the more economical methods of Farg. VIII, 8.
22. In other words: the height and length are the measure of a man, the width is one ell.
23. dàityô kata...iristahè; this expression is probably the origin of Zád-marg. marg corresponding to irista, and dád (from dàityô) having been altered to zád for the pleasure of the antithesis ("birth and death").
24. Until the fine season returns and the roads are open, the Dakhma being generally quite far from inhabited places. — In our mountains of Savoy, there are certain villages, high up in the snows, where the dead wait in the granary until the roads reopen.
25. That is, until the birds have returned.
26. nyàoñcò apa tacin, âpò being implied in nyàoñcò: the Pahlavi translates nîhân jûihc (read jûic?) bará tacêt, "that the hidden currents (?) flow." This refers to the waters that remained hidden beneath the earth during winter. — nyàoñe, originally "which is below" (cf. Skt. nyañc nie), hence: "buried, hidden" (cf. Aogemaidé, 60, 62). — Gloss: "that is to say, until the obstacle of winter has passed."
27. us vâtô zãm haècayât, "that the wind de-moistens the earth" (haècay, khûsinîtan, "to render humid," us haècayât "removes the humidity").
28. They shall expose it on the Dakhma, face toward the sky: cf. Farg. III, note 15.

29. C'est-à-dire que le crime ne peut être expié que par la vertu de la Religion, comme le crime d'ashavaghnya (Farg. III, 41), comme le crime de laisser deux ans un cadavre enfoui (voir Farg. III, 38 sq.). On verra plus loin, §§ 21-26, le genre d'expiation ordonnée dans le cas présent.
30. « Il sera en faute » tant qu'il n'aura pas porté le corps au Dakhma, ce qui est la première condition de l'expiation.
31. aiwi-varshtanâm, construit trois fois, avec nasunâm, dakhmanâm, hikhranâm. Je le considère comme un participe passé de aiwi-varsh « pleuvoir par dessus ». C'est le seul exemple verbal de varsh, ce qui fait que le Commentaire ne l'a pas reconnu et le rattache à varez « faire », madam varzishnîh, d'où il tire péniblement le sens nécessaire, celui d'enlever (barâ yadrûntan) la matière morte. Mais tout le développement qui suit (§§ 15-21) prouve jusqu'à l'évidence qu'il s'agit ici de l'action de la pluie ; et c'est ainsi que l'entend expressément l'analyse du Dinkart (l. l., § 20) : madam mas sûtih i min vârân, lvatâ vâritan pun nasâi u khazán héhr « du grand avantage de la pluie, quand il pleut sur les cadavres, les Dakhmas et les liquides impurs ». Peut-être après tout varzishnîh n'est-il qu'une faute de copiste pour vârishnîh.
32. hikhranâm : hikhra désigne l'impureté liquide du mort ou du vivant et s'oppose à nasu qui désigne l'impureté solide du mort. — hikhra vient de hic « arroser » ; devient en pehlvi héhr (afghan khîrai).

34. Vouru-kasha, Firâkh-kart (kasha = *karta), n'est pas une mer particulière : c'est l'Océan, réservoir et source de toutes les eaux. Aussi les textes ne contiennent-ils aucune donnée qui puisse le localiser et le particulariser. C'est la source d'où viennent toutes les eaux et où elles retournent : c'est aussi le siège d'un certain nombre d'êtres surnaturels : le Hôm blanc, qui doit donner l'immortalité aux morts, à l'heure de la résurrection (Minôkh., LXII, 28-30) ; l'Arbre de toutes les semences

14 (46). And if the worshippers of Mazda let a whole year pass without exposing the body to the gaze of the sun, prescribe for this crime the same penalty as for the murder of a believer 29.

And so 30 until the rain has fallen upon the corpse 31, the rain has fallen upon the Dakhma, the rain has fallen upon the impure liquids 32, and the birds have devoured the body.


III b.

15 (49). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!
Is it true that you, Ahura Mazda, draw 33 the waters of the sea Vouru-kasha 34 by means of the wind and the clouds?


29. That is to say, the crime can only be expiated through the virtue of the Religion, just as the crime of ashavaghnya (Farg. III, 41), and the crime of leaving a corpse buried for two years (see Farg. III, 38 sq.). The kind of expiation prescribed in the present case will be seen further on, §§ 21-26.
30. "He will be at fault" so long as he has not carried the body to the Dakhma, which is the first condition of expiation.
31. aiwi-varshtanâm, constructed three times, with nasunâm, dakhmanâm, hikhranâm. I take it as a past participle of aiwi-varsh, "to rain upon." It is the only verbal example of varsh, which is why the Commentary did not recognize it and connects it to varez, "to do," madam varzishnîh, from which it laboriously derives the necessary sense of removing (barâ yadrûntan) the dead matter. But the entire development that follows (§§ 15-21) proves beyond doubt that what is meant here is the action of rain; and this is indeed how the analysis in the Dinkart (l. l., § 20) understands it: madam mas sûtih i min vârân, lvatâ vâritan pun nasâi u khazán héhr, "of the great benefit of rain, when it falls upon corpses, Dakhmas, and impure liquids." Perhaps after all varzishnîh is merely a copyist's error for vârishnîh.
32. hikhranâm: hikhra denotes the liquid impurity of the dead or the living, and is opposed to nasu, which denotes the solid impurity of the dead. — hikhra comes from hic, "to sprinkle"; it becomes héhr in Pahlavi (Afghan khîrai).
33. zahâhi, vakhdûné.
34. Vouru-kasha, Firâkh-kart (kasha = *karta), is not a particular sea: it is the Ocean, reservoir and source of all waters. Accordingly, the texts contain no data that would allow it to be localized or particularized. It is the source from which all waters come and to which they return; it is also the dwelling-place of a number of supernatural beings: the white Hôm, which is to grant immortality to the dead at the hour of resurrection (Minôkh., LXII, 28-30); the Tree of all seeds

et l'oiseau Saêna qui les disperse au vent (Yt. XII, 17; Minókh., ibid., 37 sq.); l'Ane à trois pieds qui purifie les eaux de la mer Vouru-kasha (Yasna XLII, 4; Minôkh., ibid., 26; cf. vol. I, 276, note 7). — Le nom Vouru-kasha semble signifier littéralement, soit [la mer] « faite large » (si kasha = kereta), soit « aux profondeurs larges » (kasha *karta = sscr. karta « fosse »).

35. frazayayâhi, shabkûné (c'est-à-dire هيل). — Comment donc peux-tu défendre de laisser la matière morte toucher l'eau (cf. § 15; Vd. VI, 26-41; VII, 25-27), puisque toi, le premier, tu fais tomber l'eau sur les cadavres?

36. anhaithim, an-âshkârâk.

37. La mer Pûitika est la mer où les eaux du Vouru-kasha, souillées sur la terre, vont se purifier pour repasser de là dans la mer Vouru-kasha et rentrer dans la circulation générale. « Toute la grossièreté, l'amertume, l'impureté (satparih, sûrih, lâ dakyâih) de la mer Pûtik essaye de passer dans la mer Frâkh-kart, mais un vent fort et haut soufflant du Var Satvês les repousse; tout ce qu'il y a de pur et de mobile passe dans la mer Frâkh-kart et dans les sources d'Ardvisûr et le reste (l'élément impur) reflue dans la mer Pûtik » (Bund. XII, 10). Ce va-et-vient qui emporte l'eau purifiée au Frâkh-kart et ramène au Pûtik l'eau impure et amère, c'est-à-dire l'eau salée, est évidemment le flux et le reflux. Toutes les eaux vont à la mer et elles en reviennent pures et sans amertume sous forme de pluie et d'eau de rivière : on imagina que c'est le mouvement de la marée qui opère cette division.

38. ghzhare-ghzharentish, dar apakhshik dûr adâsht mâlâ.

16 (51). That you carry them over the corpses, you, Ahura Mazda? That you carry them over the Dakhma, you, Ahura Mazda? That you carry them over the impure liquids, you, Ahura Mazda? That you let them fall 35 upon the bones, you, Ahura Mazda? And that you make them return, in an invisible manner 36, you, Ahura Mazda: that you make them return to the sea Pûitika 37.

17 (53). Ahura Mazda replied:

Exactly as you say, O pure Zarathushtra.

I, Ahura Mazda, take the waters of the sea Vourukaska, with the aid of the wind and the clouds.

18 (55). I carry them over the corpses, I, Ahura Mazda; I carry them over the Dakhma, I, Ahura Mazda; I carry them over the impure liquids, I, Ahura Mazda; I let them fall upon the bones, I, Ahura Mazda. And I make them return, in an invisible manner, I, Ahura Mazda: I make them return to the sea Pûitika.

19 (56). The waters stop and swell 38 at the heart of the sea [Pûitika], and having purified themselves there, flow from the sea Pûitika to the sea Vourukasha,

and the bird Saêna who disperses them in the wind (Yt. XII, 17; Minókh., ibid., 37 sq.); the three-legged Ass who purifies the waters of the sea Vouru-kasha (Yasna XLII, 4; Minôkh., ibid., 26; cf. vol. I, 276, note 7). — The name Vouru-kasha seems to mean literally, either [the sea] "made wide" (if kasha = kereta), or "of wide depths" (kasha *karta = Sanskrit karta "pit").

35. frazayayâhi, shabkûné (that is to say, هيل). — How then can you defend allowing dead matter to touch the water (cf. § 15; Vd. VI, 26-41; VII, 25-27), since you yourself, in the first place, make the water fall upon the corpses?

36. anhaithim, an-âshkârâk.

37. The sea Pûitika is the sea where the waters of the Vouru-kasha, defiled upon the earth, go to purify themselves in order to pass back from there into the sea Vouru-kasha and re-enter the general circulation. "All the grossness, the bitterness, the impurity (satparih, sûrih, lâ dakyâih) of the sea Pûtik tries to pass into the sea Frâkh-kart, but a strong and high wind blowing from the Var Satvês drives them back; everything that is pure and mobile passes into the sea Frâkh-kart and into the springs of Ardvisûr, and the remainder (the impure element) flows back into the sea Pûtik" (Bund. XII, 10). This back-and-forth movement which carries the purified water to the Frâkh-kart and brings back the impure, bitter water — that is, salt water — to the Pûtik, is evidently the ebb and flow of the tide. All waters go to the sea and return from it pure and without bitterness in the form of rain and river water: it was imagined that it is the movement of the tides that brings about this division.

38. ghzhare-ghzharentish, dar apakhshik dûr adâsht mâlâ.

IV c.

21 (63). "What you say, O pure one, that is indeed the good thing, that is indeed the beautiful thing."

By this word, the holy Ahura Mazda gladdened the holy Zarathushtra 41. Purity is, after birth, the first good thing for man 42; purity, O Zarathushtra, which is in the Religion of Mazda, the purity of the man who purifies himself with good thoughts, good words, and good deeds.

22 (68). Creator of the corporeal world, holy one!

Of what greatness, of what goodness, of what beauty is the Law hostile to the Daêvas, the law of Zarathushtra 43 — is it not greater, better, and more beautiful than all other Words?

39. hvâpâm, hû-âp: this is the Tree of all seeds; see Yt. XII, 17.
40. Shaken down by the bird Cañmrôsh: see the citation from the Minôkhard, Yt. XII, 17.
41. Gloss: "When Zartûsht saw that man can, through virtue, escape the state of sin, he was joyful." — Ahura's approval doubtless refers to a development of Zoroaster concerning the efficacy of the Law in saving the faithful.
42. yaozhdâo mashyâi aipi zâthem vahishtâ: a Gathic formula, Yasna XLVIII, 5 c. — Purity, that is to say the purification of body and soul: cf. Farg. X, 18.
43. The analysis of the Dinkart seems to see here the Vendidad itself: (madam masih u sha-pirihi Jût Shêdâ Dât pun shûyishn min apârik srav: "of the greatness and goodness of the Vendidad above the other Words in the work of purification"). But this does not concern our book of the Vendidad; it concerns, in a general way, the part of the Law destined for the struggle against the Divs, the legal part (dâd), as opposed to the other parts of the Avesta, the other divine Words (gâsân and hâdak-mânsarik; cf. Dinkart VIII, 1, 5).

61. Literally "a young dog," but used only of the hunting dog (Farg. XIII, 8): Lagarde (Symmicta, 263) connects it with the Persian tôla meaning "small dog" and "hunting dog."
62. sukuruna, sukar; is probably the porcupine, Persian sugârûn, سکارون, Afghan shkôn (Afghan n = rn; see Chants populaires des Afghans, XLVII), the Baragsta dialect has سکل which is the Pahlavi form.
63. The Commentary reproduces the names Jazhu, Aiwizu, Vizu without translating them, with the gloss là rôshnak meaning "unknown." According to the Bundahish, XIV, 19, the dog family comprises ten species: the shepherd dog, the guard dog, the Vohunazg, the hunting dog (tarûk = tauruna), the beaver (bawrak miâîk = bawrish upàpô), the fox (rûpás = raopi), the weasel (raspûk, urupi), the hedgehog (zûzak, duzhaka), the porcupine (sûkar, sukuruna), and the musk deer (mûshkân).

text:
ZEND-AVESTA : VENDIDAD. — FARGARD 5 77

Si c'est une belette 64, combien de créatures du Bon Esprit souille-t-elle par contact direct? combien en souille-t-elle par contact indirect ?

34 (110). Ahura Mazda répondit :

La belette ne souille aucune des créatures du Bon Esprit, ni par contact direct, ni par contact indirect, excepté celui qui la frappe et la tue : à celle-là elle s'attache 65 pour toujours et à tout jamais 66.

35 (113). Créateur du monde des corps, saint !

Si c'est un bandit, un méchant bipède, par exemple un impie Ashemaogha 65, combien des créatures du Bon Esprit souille-t-elle par contact direct, combien par contact indirect ?

36 (115). Ahura Mazda répondit :

Autant qu'une grenouille 67 toute desséchée 66 et morte de plus d'une année. C'est pendant qu'il est vivant, ô Spitama Zarathushtra, qu'un bandit, un méchant bipède, par exemple un impie Ashemaogha, souille les créatures du Bon Esprit par contact direct, les souille par contact indirect 68.

37 (119). Vivant, il frappe l'eau ; vivant, il éteint le feu 69 ; vivant, il détourne et emmène le bétail 70 ; vivant, il frappe le fidèle d'un coup qui enlève les sens 71, qui sépare l'âme du corps : mort, il ne le fait plus.

38 (120). Vivant, ô Spitama Zarathushtra, un bandit, un méchant bipède, par exemple un impie Ashemaogha, enlève au fidèle la jouissance 72 des ali-

64. spa urupi, rapûk (lire raspûk) ; Frâmji a noliu « belette » ; raspûk (cf. Vd. pehlvi, I, 17, 65) est le p. راسو ; les brouillons d'Anquetil ont rassu.

65. C'est-à-dire elle le souille (âhûkinêt).

66. En ce sens que la souillure ne se communique pas de lui à autrui. Il peut d'ailleurs s'en purifier.

66. Un hérétique : voir vol. I, p. 91, note 55.

67. vazagha, vazagh ; une des créatures d'Ahriman les plus détestées ; cf. Farg. XIV, 5 et note 15. — vish-hushkô = vi-hushka; peut-être * vish « poison » (sscr. visha), auquel cas vish--hushkò serait « dont le poison est desséché ».

69. Il souille l'eau en y portant des impuretés. — Éteindre le feu était, selon Strabon, puni de mort (probablement quand il s'agit de feu sacré); cf. Farg. VII, 25.

70. gâm varatâm azaiti : cf. Farg. III, 11, note 17.

71. frazâ-baodhanhem : cf. Farg. IV, 40, note 9.

72. hanhéush ou anhéush, sîrih (cf. Yasna, LIII, 4 c et note 18). En souillant les objets usuels, il les rend hors d'usage pour le fidèle.
translation:
ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — FARGARD 5 77

If it is a weasel, how many creatures of the Good Spirit does it defile by direct contact? How many does it defile by indirect contact?

34 (110). Ahura Mazda answered:

The weasel defiles none of the creatures of the Good Spirit, neither by direct contact nor by indirect contact, except for the one who strikes and kills it: to that person it attaches itself forever and for all time.

35 (113). Creator of the world of bodies, holy one!

If it is a bandit, a wicked biped, for example an impious Ashemaogha, how many of the creatures of the Good Spirit does it defile by direct contact, how many by indirect contact?

36 (115). Ahura Mazda answered:

As much as a frog, entirely dried up and dead for more than a year. It is while he is alive, O Spitama Zarathushtra, that a bandit, a wicked biped, for example an impious Ashemaogha, defiles the creatures of the Good Spirit by direct contact and defiles them by indirect contact.

37 (119). While alive, he strikes the water; while alive, he extinguishes the fire; while alive, he drives away and steals the cattle; while alive, he strikes the faithful with a blow that takes away their senses, separating the soul from the body: when dead, he does none of this.

38 (120). While alive, O Spitama Zarathushtra, a bandit, a wicked biped, for example an impious Ashemaogha, takes away from the faithful the enjoyment of ali-

64. spa urupi, rapûk (read raspûk); Frâmji gives noliu meaning "weasel"; raspûk (cf. Vd. pehlvi, I, 17, 65) is the Persian راسو; Anquetil's drafts have rassu.

65. That is to say, it defiles him (âhûkinêt).

66. In the sense that the defilement is not transmitted from him to others. He can moreover purify himself from it.

66. A heretic: see vol. I, p. 91, note 55.

67. vazagha, vazagh; one of the most detested creatures of Ahriman; cf. Farg. XIV, 5 and note 15. — vish-hushkô = vi-hushka; perhaps * vish meaning "poison" (Sanskrit visha), in which case vish-hushkò would mean "one whose poison is dried up."

68. "Because those who approach him become worse": he corrupts them.

69. He defiles the water by casting impurities into it. — Extinguishing fire was, according to Strabo, punishable by death (probably when it concerns sacred fire); cf. Farg. VII, 25.

70. gâm varatâm azaiti: cf. Farg. III, 11, note 17.

71. frazâ-baodhanhem: cf. Farg. IV, 40, note 9.

72. hanhéush or anhéush, sîrih (cf. Yasna, LIII, 4 c and note 18). By defiling everyday objects, he renders them unfit for use by the faithful.
